#913. Lens were humiliated by Como. The pain continued against Marseille

Pierre Sage led Lens to second and glory in the Coupe de France last season. A lot has changed in the last six months

The Lens striker, Florian Sotoca, was completely motionless as he looked into the middle space from the bench. The game, finely poised at 2-1 with a few minutes remaining, was not beyond his side, but that is not the story his troubled face told.

Marseille had just restored their lead thanks to a goal from substitute Keyliane Abdallah. Bruno Génésio’s men would go on to take all three points and continue their unlikely charge up the table, but the atmosphere at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis was morose before Marseille had even stepped on the pitch. The match did little to lift the mood at the end of a week in which Lens made unwanted history.

A pre-match banner unfurled by Lens fans that called the players a “disgrace” had not even been put away when a miscommunication between Jonathan Gradit and Samson Baidoo gifted Marseille the lead after 82 seconds. The former’s pass dribbled towards the goalline and was tapped in by Amine Gouiri from just a yard out.

It was a disastrous start for Lens, who recorded the joint-heaviest defeat in Champions League history last week. The 9-1 thrashing by Como was also the heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. Yannick Cahuzac, the Lens manager, called it a “humiliation”. The club’s president, Joseph Oughourlian, scrawled the words: “never again” inside the dressing room. Losing to Marseille on Sunday was not as chastening but the defeat posed more questions about the club’s recent decisions.

When Cahuzac, a friend of sporting director Jean-Louis Leca, stepped up from his assistant role in September to replace Dino Toppmöller, who lasted just six games, there were accusations of cronyism. Cahuzac’s stint so far has been a poor advert for the practice.

After three defeats in the league, winless in the Champions League, a derby defeat to Lille, a record-breaking loss to Como, and the wheels have well and truly come off at Lens; the jury is out on whether Cahuzac can set them back in motion. It was one of his former teammates, Florian Thauvin, who equalised for Lens against Marseille – his former club – with a close-range header. The playmaker, a harsh omission from Zinedine Zidane’s latest France squad, has been a rare bright spot in an increasingly gloomy situation.

Génésio said earlier in the season that these were the kinds of games Marseille could compete in but not win. But, as the French maxim goes, “le foot va vite” (football moves quickly). The tide has turned in Marseille; five league wins in a row have taken Marseille from the relegation zone to the Champions League places.

Génésio says his team’s fragile revival exists on “a knife’s edge”, however recent results – including a win at Bayer Leverkusen in the Europa League last week – have fed into growing optimism that his limited squad (both in quality and quantity) might avoid the abject season that fans had assumed was inevitable. The achievement belongs to Génésio, as does this win, secured by substitute Abdallah.

The academy product was banished to the reserves after his performance against Le Havre last month. Génésio criticised “a kind of lobbying around the young players” (from whom he did not specify) and held firm on his stance. He got the desired response. Re-integrated, Abdallah popped up at the back post to give Marseille a win that has taken them up to fourth in the table. They were second from bottom before the last international break.

Lens have replaced Marseille as France’s crisis club. After the match the home players did a tour of the pitch, applauding the fans for their support. In response, the fans unfurled a banner that read: “Shame on you.” Le foot va vite. Just six months ago fans packed into the Bollaert in the wee hours of the morning to welcome home their heroes after they had won the Coupe de France final. That feels like a lifetime ago for the players, fans and Pierre Sage, the manager who delivered that trophy.

“We are sick,” admitted Cahuzac after the match. There has been soul-searching but also plenty of finger pointing. Cahuzac says he “isn’t worried” about his job. Despite the growing pressure, he certainly has reasons to feel reassured but his friend, Léca, is also under a bit of fire after a second summer transfer window considerably less successful than his first. Jean-Clair Todibo, Thorgan Hazard and Franjo Ivanovic all arrived with high expectations but have fallen way short of them.

The fans had a banner for Léca, too, calling out his “shit interview” after the defeat to Como. They wanted an “apology”. They did not get one but it is certainly a sorry state of affairs at Lens.

Monaco won their third game in a row in the Conference League last week, but their 1-1 draw at Le Mans was their fifth straight game without a win in Ligue 1. Filipe Luís says they need to “cleanse the minds” over the international break. When Monaco last won in Ligue 1 – against Lens in September – they were top of the table. They now sit seventh. The goals have dried up for Paris Brunner, Folarin Balogun – returning from injury – has yet to replicate the form that attracted Premier League interest and Matthis Abline put in an anonymous display against Le Mans. Monaco were reliant on a defensive blunder to open the scoring through Mamadou Coulibaly, who could be in trouble for a throat-slit celebration. Brunner was punished for a similar celebration earlier this season, although on that occasion it was directed towards the opposition fans. Le Mans, who equalised in the 90th minute through Erwan Colas, are also without a league win since September, but there was a strong show of support for manager Patrick Videira from the home fans, who also took a dig at the club’s unpopular football adviser Bruno Cheyrou. He evidently would not have popular support if he were to instigate a managerial change.

From cleansing minds at Monaco to exorcising demons at Nice. The club endured a shocking 2025-26 campaign, during which the relationship between fans, the players, and the club reached breaking point. It ended with Nice narrowly avoiding relegation to Ligue 2, thanks to a playoff win over Saint-Étienne. A new manager, Olivier Pantaloni, and a new sporting director, Roger Ricort, came in over the summer, but the players and Pantaloni continued to speak of the scars of the previous campaign. They showed in the opening four games, none of which Le Gym managed to win. Since then, however, only PSG have taken more points. Nice’s 2-0 win at Angers means they have picked up 15 points from their last possible 18. The club are now in European contention. Pantaloni is once again working his magic, just as he did at Lorient last season.

#912. 'The worst conditions in my 35-year career' - commentating in the FA Cup fog

Notts County beat Altrincham in incredible fog-filled spectacle

One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday.

As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two.

"One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience.

"I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the second round and the fog came in.

"Tonight was worse. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing.

"We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging.

"I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can."

Notts County progress in FA Cup tie no-one could see

'It's like a fever dream' - commentators struggle through fog

National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties.

"The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower.

"It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it.

"Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible."

Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition.

"I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!"

Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Altrincham have a rich history of causing FA Cup upsets but could not add to that in the fog against Notts County

The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window.

"[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower.

"Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Have they changed shape? Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'.

"So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well.

"It was very, very close to getting called off."

Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle.

"It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale.

"You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in."

The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction".

"Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around."

#910. 'I can't believe he is one of us' - inside Salah's life in Trabzon

Mohamed Salah has scored 10 goals in 15 games for Turkish club Trabzonspor

Back in August, when Mohamed Salah landed in Istanbul after flying in from his holiday in Mykonos, he wore Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue home strip as he stepped out of the plane to be greeted by thousands of fans.

That kit sold out almost instantly. Later that day, as Salah headed to Trabzon in north-east Turkey to complete the formalities of one of the most unexpected transfers after the expiry of his Liverpool contract, he asked one of his entourage what he should wear.

"The same kit," came the response, but Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan advised Salah to wear the black away kit instead. Of course, that sold out too.

From the outset of the 34-year-old's arrival to this historic port city on the Black Sea, that sense of adulation has only grown.

"I went to the airport to see him in Istanbul and it was surreal," says Nisa Dumangoz. "I still can't believe that he is one of us."

Go for a stroll through Trabzon on matchday and it is Salah's face which adorns everything. Even the walls inside the fishmongers have pictures of him.

At the club shop in town, one of the staff jokes that the ground floor is for the Egyptian and the upper floor is for everything else.

Outside the stadium, there are scarves, magnets, keyrings, lighters with his face on and Egyptian Nemes headdresses in Trabzonspor colours. Season ticket sales rocketed after his arrival.

"Walking around Trabzon, it feels as though nine out of every 10 fans wearing a shirt have Salah's name on the back. The 10th has their own," says Turkish football journalist Hasan Tuncel.

The club have surpassed their merchandise revenue from last year in three months since Salah's arrival, while the local airport is only getting busier.

Liverpool was difficult to reach for many supporters across the Arab world and tickets were often hard to source. Trabzon is far more accessible, with new flights introduced from Cairo, Dubai and Riyadh since Salah's arrival.

On our flight from Istanbul, we meet an Egyptian family of 10 coming from Cairo for Trabzonspor's Uefa Conference League game against Freiburg.

"He is our ambassador and our Egyptian King, and with how many people want to come to Turkey now, he is their ambassador too," says Mahmoud.

At the game, there is a group of Egyptian celebrities and influencers. A quick check of their social media shows their combined Instagram following of about five million. Trabzonspor have three million. Salah has 68 million.

Salah recently went for a hike and posed for a picture on a rock in the Trabzon highlands. That rock has been renamed Salahtasi (Salah's Rock) and is now a tourist destination.

The commercial element of his signing has more than been justified but crucially, on the pitch, Salah is driving Trabzonspor's push for the Turkish Super Lig title and he has hit the ground running with 10 goals and five assists in all competitions.

Trabzonspor trail leaders Galatasaray by three points, having won seven of their first 10 games, including victories against the table-toppers and Besiktas.

For context, the Istanbul 'big three' of Galatasaray (26), Fenerbahce (19) and Besiktas (16) have won the league on 61 occasions combined, compared with Trabzonspor's seven titles.

"In Turkey, he is the biggest football star after Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo," says Kerim Tonyali, who is part of Gurbetci Gencler, a Trabzonspor supporters' group.

And given Salah's status as an icon, Trabzonspor are quickly becoming the second club for many in Turkey and the wider Muslim world.

Salah's face is a common sight wherever you go in Trabzon

Trabzon may be more than 2,000 miles from Liverpool but there are similarities, particularly when it comes to the sense of identity and pride associated with originating from here.

"Everywhere is Trabzon for us," is the local mantra and aligns with the sense of unity within this city that has a population of about 800,000 and is only the 30th-biggest in Turkey.

For Salah, the financials were important and he is earning about Â£14.6m per year as well as 20% of official merchandise sold with his name on, but one of the key aspects of coming here was the ability to focus entirely on his football.

Besiktas was considered as an option after the 2026 World Cup but, after multiple calls with Trabzonspor, Salah felt they were the ideal fit and offered a life away from the hustle and bustle of Istanbul.

He has his own security detail and is living in the nearby town of Yomra, where he now has a street named after him. He also employs a private chef and, unsurprisingly, continues to set standards in the gym and on the training ground.

By all accounts, Salah is thriving. He is a fan of Turkish coffee and is often spotted leaving the ground with Ayran - a traditional yogurt drink - but as much as he wants to explore the city, he knows of the difficulties given his reputation.

"Everyone wants to work with a star like Mohamed Salah," said Trabzonspor's Paul Onuachu, formerly of Southampton. "He adds so much and helps all of us and he contributes positively. I am grateful for him. It's a blessing to play with him."

Watching Salah in the flesh in a Conference League game against Freiburg, his pace has gone down a notch compared with his peak but the touch, quick feet and sheer quality is still there. And so is that knack of getting in goalscoring positions, even if his defensive duties - which were such a source of debate last season at Liverpool - are limited.

Salah believes he still has plenty to give for club and country, with aspirations to play in both the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations and 2030 World Cup, which will be partly held in North Africa.

No decision has been made about how long he will stay in Turkey, but there is growing belief among sources in the Middle East that he will move to Saudi Arabia when his two-year Trabzonspor deal expires in 2028. By then, he will be 36.

Salah signed a two-year deal with Trabzonspor in the summer of 2026

On initial thoughts, it is easy to question how and why Salah ended up here.

When he delivered that infamous mixed-zone interview at Leeds' Elland Road less than a year ago and the wheels of his departure from Liverpool were set in motion, surely no-one would have imagined his next destination would be this Turkish outpost near the Georgian border.

"I remember looking at him when we landed in Trabzon and seeing the crowds outside and how emotional it was," says Anil Dincer, one of the lawyers involved in Salah's move to Turkey.

"We already have Salah and Fabinho. So now we are waiting for [Virgil] Van Dijk," adds Serhat Sumer, a Trabzonspor fan.

Salah, of course, delivered so much joy to Liverpool and the intention here is the same. This is no drift towards retirement, but a player determined to prove he still belongs at the highest level and that football still has meaning beyond trophies and money.

Asked by BBC Sport if he had a message for Liverpool fans, Salah simply said "hello" and smiled. Given how rarely he spoke in the mixed zone during his time at Anfield, it is not in his nature to talk regularly on record.

Last season was Salah's least prolific at Anfield, but given Liverpool's struggles in front of goal in the Premier League, it is hard to argue they have replaced one of their greatest ever players.

Perhaps a time will come when the likes of Salah, Arne Slot and Richard Hughes will reveal more about the chain of events that led to the forward agreeing to terminate his contract a year early. As it is, none of them are at the club and that chapter is firmly closed.

Salah's influence that once helped shape the Premier League is now being felt on the shores of the Black Sea. He is Trabzonspor's force of nature. And the team known as the Black Sea Storm are rising and on the hunt for silverware with their Egyptian King.

#909. Evanilson ignites eighth straight Bournemouth win at blundering Ipswich

Marco Rose paid tribute to his Bournemouth side after a hard‑fought 2-1 victory at Ipswich equalled the club’s record of eight consecutive wins.

Evanilson got the ball rolling after five minutes, scoring for a fifth successive Premier League match. With seven goals this season, he has already beaten his tally from the whole of last season.

His latest was a gift from the Ipswich goalkeeper, Christian Walton, who tried and failed to dribble past ­him in the area, and Bournemouth went two up after 27 seconds of the second half when Leif Davis could only deflect Ryan Christie’s strike into his own net.

Lewis Cook tripped Abdoul ­Ouattara in the area to provide the hosts with a lifeline and Jack Clarke scored the penalty with 17 minutes left to set up a grandstand finish at Portman Road.

However, Bournemouth stood firm to make it eight wins in a row and match the record set under Eddie Howe in 2012-13, a season which ended with promotion from League One.

Speaking after a win which came three days after a victorious journey to Sparta Prague, Rose said: “I am pleased with the first 70 minutes because we went two up and I didn’t feel like we struggled or can get any problems, but it’s [the] Premier League and one goal changed the momentum of the game.

“That is why I am much more pleased with the last 20 minutes. We suffered but we did it together.”

A slow start last month at Chelsea proved costly for Bournemouth, and even in last weekend’s 2-0 home win against Leeds the visitors had an effort ruled out after 11 minutes. That made goals at the start of each half particularly sweet for Rose.

“Last week I said we start slow and this week I said we start quite quick and score an early goal. I am a magician!” the German said with a smile. “No, we know we have to be ready in this league. We played Chelsea four weeks ago and we were two down after three minutes. That’s why we learned and always good to score an early goal.

“We were sharp, we were good and that’s what I really appreciate. I said before this week that it’s going to be really demanding for a team that is not used to have this kind of [­European] situation.”

Julio Enciso went close late on with two free‑kicks, but this defeat means Ipswich have only won one of their last seven in all competitions.

Gary O’Neil, their manager, said: “[We are] gutted with the result, firstly, because it’s what we are here for and probably performance-wise not much in it. To lose a football match you’ve not been outclassed in is hard to take. But if you give the ball to the opposition No 9 twice, it’s going to be difficult and that was the story of the game really.

“It’s the level so we have to find a way of not only being competitive in games, but can we now find a way to make sure these Hull [a 2-2 draw] and Bournemouth performances are four points and not one.”

#908. Falkirk add goals and grit to McGlynn's guile on rapid rise

Falkirk raced into a 4-0 half-time lead away to Hearts

In the space of a week Falkirk have beaten defending champions Celtic and become the first team to get the better of Hearts in a Scottish Premiership match at Tynecastle in 19 months, scoring a combined seven goals in the process.

The 5-2 success in Edinburgh was their fifth successive victory and takes John McGlynn's side up to third place.

A month ago, the concession of an added time goal to Dundee left them 11th, only a point off the bottom of the table.

"It's striking a balance without getting carried away and not playing it down too much," McGlynn told BBC Scotland.

"Winning five games in a row, you've obviously got something about you. We want it to continue because we're enjoying this.

"But we're only 13 games in. There's a long way to go, so we've got to keep our feet on the ground and enjoy seeing our team third in the league."

The 64-year-old earned plaudits aplenty last season for guiding Falkirk to sixth on their return to the top flight after overseeing consecutive promotions.

Liam Henderson, who scored the sublime fourth goal against Hearts, was with the Bairns in those League One days, as were Brad Spencer and Ethan Ross.

Unused substitutes Finn Yeats and Ross MacIver have been on the journey with McGlynn too, as has Leon McCann, who missed out through injury.

"We've got a good team spirit, a togetherness, and a will to work hard for your team-mates," said centre-half Henderson. "We now have a ruthlessness up front as well.

"The manager is massive to us. His knowledge, his detail. He is so detailed in everything he does.

"We're breaking records this season and creating some history. A lot of pundits and fans were saying that we weren't the team we were last year."

There is truth to that. While some of the old guard remain, there was a huge squad turnover in the summer.

Calvin Miller went to Hearts, Dylan Tait is now the skipper at Dundee United and Barney Stewart, who scored 10 goals between January and May, was sold to West Bromwich Albion for a club record fee.

Loan players Filip Lissah, Ben Broggio, Henry Cartwright, Kyrell Wilson, Ethan Williams and Louie Marsh said their goodbyes.

John McGlynn has taken maximum points from two games against his old team Hearts this season

McGlynn brought in a whopping 17 new faces, with Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames and Jacob Murrell, who all scored against Hearts, arriving weeks after the campaign had kicked off.

Murrell, 22, picked up the SPFL player of the month award for October and his Tynecastle double takes his tally to seven, making him joint-top scorer in the division.

"They look at what kind of player fits into the team and when the player arrives, they know what they're getting," said former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart in praise of Falkirk's scouting.

Meanwhile, former Hibs midfielder Scott Allan highlighted captain Spencer as the "heartbeat" of the team.

"You need a guy like him in there to really set the standards," Allan said of the 30-year-old midfielder, who followed McGlynn from Raith Rovers.

"When he is in the team, there is a real control from Falkirk, especially in the middle.

"They've added a steeliness to the team too, it's not always total football this year. They are able to do the dirty side of the game now and roll up the sleeves when they have to."

McGlynn is very much the unassuming star of the show though.

"He is a manager who is totally comfortable in his own skin now," said Stewart.

"He exudes confidence. Perhaps before he was considered a bit of an unfashionable manager. I mean in terms of stature, and not in what he's doing on the park.

"The perception of him continues to get better and better.

"I don't want to be disrespectful to Falkirk, but I would not be surprised, if, when one or two of the bigger jobs start coming up, rather than being an outsider, I think he will be right in the hunt for some of those."

As things stand, almost any move away from Falkirk would be a step down the league.

#907. Le Fée’s penalty stuns Chelsea and breathes life into defiant Sunderland

A lot can change in five‑and‑a‑half months, but as an early winter chill descended on Wearside last week – both meteorologically and ­metaphorically – Sunderland were determined that some things should remain the same. Just as they had beaten Chelsea on the final day of last season to ensure European qualification for the first time in 53 years, they did so again on Sunday to lift themselves off the bottom of the Premier League.

The Sunderland performance was certainly familiar to their head coach, Régis Le Bris – “the identity, the intensity, the togetherness, the way we managed the game” – on the way to three crucial points.

Ultimately a patched-up defence, ­without the injured Dan Ballard and the banned Omar Alderete, kept ­Chelsea at enough distance to allow Robin Roefs a tranquil ­afternoon amid the tumult. Chelsea may be ­developing into a ­chaotic must‑watch under Xabi Alonso but they were ­subdued here and have fallen out of the top four. “We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win,” Alonso said. “We lacked a bit of patience and creativity.”

Margins were paper-thin in a game decided by two first-half penalty calls, the first not awarded to Chelsea after Luke O’Nien’s clumsy challenge on Cole Palmer, deemed after video assistant referee consideration to be fractionally outside the area, and the second given to the hosts by Jarred Gillett after Levi Colwill brought down the ebullient Brian Brobbey; the defender argued, not without justification, that the Dutch striker had a handful of his shirt too but the award stood.

Alonso, as ever, made no excuses, ­focusing not on the officiating and more on how he was “not happy with how we defended that situation”. Enzo Le Fée had been equally unequi­vocal just beyond the half‑hour, sending Mike Penders the wrong way and dispatching into the goalkeeper’s bottom-right corner for the game’s only goal.

Europe may be a blessing for Sunderland but the full-time mood had been bleak after the latest alarming performance in the home defeat against Dinamo Zagreb on Thursday. It had felt like a season watershed and only the captain, Granit Xhaka, Thomas Meunier and Roefs survived the cull here. That the talismanic Xhaka, the subject of strong summer interest from his former coach Alonso, had his afternoon truncated by injury after less than three ­minutes, felt like yet more of the ill fortune dogging Sunderland.

There was no feeling sorry for themselves, though. With this the start of a challenging quartet of fixtures leading into the Tyne‑Wear derby next month, it felt like this match had to be attacked to prevent an early-season hiccup turning into a full mid‑season tangle with relegation trouble. And Chelsea were greeted with determination and ­aggression, with Xhaka’s withdrawal not ­blowing that plan off course. Two zesty ­incisions by Chemsdine Talbi in the opening quarter-hour, in his first ­Premier League start this season, caused Alonso’s men flutters, the first leading to a blocked Trai Hume shot and the second presenting Brobbey with a clear opening that he would have expected to convert.

The passion was there, the precision maybe less so. O’Nien’s challenge on Palmer elicited a penalty appeal that did not end up being costly after the VAR check and Morgan Rogers headed wide from a Marco Palestra cross, but Chelsea could not capitalise on any potential home nerves. If anyone was prone to belated Halloween frights it was the Blues, particularly at the hands of Brobbey, who led the line with enormous presence. He took on and beat the last man Wesley Fofana before steering his shot just too high, past Penders’ near post, and then won the penalty that led to Le Fée’s winner. “He is stoppable,” Alonso said, “but only when you defend better than we did.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Such was Chelsea’s bluntness in the first 45 that the coach opted for not just a substitution but a reshuffle at the break, with Estêvão replacing the injured Colwill, beefing up the attack with Moisés Caicedo slotting into the defence. Sunderland continued to fight tooth and nail in a game that threatened occasionally to bubble over. Meunier was booked for a late tackle on Caicedo and shortly afterwards Brobbey was cautioned for wrestling Roméo Lavia to the ground, a continuation of an ongoing feud between the pair. When he was substituted, spent, for the ­enduringly ­popular Wilson Isidor halfway through the second half Chelsea must have breathed a sigh of relief.

Estêvão made one burst through the middle on to a Rogers pass but Reinildo Mandava stepped across to snuff out the opportunity. Yet even with little possession Sunderland looked sharper. A ball broke for Isidor after Chelsea failed to clear Le Fée’s through ball, Penders saving and the rebound not breaking for the Frenchman before Pep Chavarría cleared.

As the last 10 minutes approached Alonso sent on Geovany Quenda for Chavarría, and the young winger finally conjured a goal attempt worthy of the description, fizzing a shot just wide of Roefs’s far post via deflection. Talbi, finishing as he started, pinged one just wide from distance on the break as the home side still looked more likely, even with a third of possession. Sunderland had rewarded their crowd’s vociferous faith.

#906. Friedel group completes Shrewsbury Town takeover

Roland Wycherley has been Shrewsbury Town owner and chairman since 1996

Shrewsbury Town's long-drawn-out takeover deal has been completed, allowing former USA international goalkeeper Brad Friedel to come in as the Shropshire outfit's new sporting director.

The paperwork on the share purchase agreement with Scott Davidson's American-based consortium Biscayne ST LLC - which includes Friedel - has been finalised, taking up 87.4 per cent of the League Two club's shares and allowing long-time owner Roland Wycherley to finally let go.

Miami-based businessman Davidson is joined on the new Town board by New York financier Will Dotson and Craig Graham, chairman of Spartans, the Edinburgh-based Scottish League Two club, while former Liverpool, Blackburn Rovers, Aston Villa and Tottenham Hotspur keeper Friedel will come in to take a hands-on role, working with manager Gavin Cowan.

Davidson becomes chairman of the board, which still includes existing members Liam Dooley, the club's chief executive, and Duncan Montgomery, while another ex-goalkeeper, Bryan Finnerty, is to join the group, pending the EFL's owners and directors' tests.

After 30 years of leading the Shropshire club, since succeeding Ray Bailey as chairman in the summer of 1996, Wycherley can now retire at the age of 85.

The Shrewsbury-born lifelong fan first made his intention clear to sell more than five years ago when the Town were still a League One club.

But his dogged determination to do a deal he had to be convinced was right for the club's long-term future before he handed over the reins has made the Shropshire businessman a tough adversary - and lengthened the process, to the frustration of Town fans.

In a club statement,, external Wycherley said his ownership tenure had been "an honour and a privilege" but admitted the club "needed new investment".

Shrewsbury Town takeover completed - looking back at last 30 years

We took our time, says Shrewsbury Town owner Wycherley

After suffering relegation in his first season, Shrewsbury have since been relegated three more times - and promoted three times - in Wycherley's period as owner.

But the biggest legacy of his three decades at the helm was the Town's move in 2007 from their old Gay Meadow home to a new 10,000 all-seater stadium.

The first of those three promotions was under Graham Turner, who returned to the club to recreate the success they had in the late 1970s and early 1980s, taking them up in 2012.

"Roland has put an awful lot into the football club," Turner told BBC Radio Shropshire. "He's kept it going, when at times it's been hard.

"I've nothing but admiration for him. Over the years he's done a very good job."

Wycherley's last game watching the club while at the helm was Saturday's 2-1 FA Cup first-round win at non-league Eastleigh.

Wycherley leaves Town lying 15th in the table, but they are only two points shy of a play-off place and have performed encouragingly this season under manager Gavin Cowan, who came back to the club in January to save them from the drop.

Town were up to eighth when they won at Crawley on 20 October - and have only slipped down in a tightly-congested table thanks to a late Rotherham equaliser followed by a late Gillingham winner a week later.

Friedel was in attendance at Oteley Road for Town's EFL Trophy Northern Group E win over Everton Under-21s on 27 October. And both he and Davidson are expected to be in attendance for this Saturday's home game with another promotion-winning former Town manager Micky Mellon's Oldham Athletic.

Brad Friedel spent the majority of his previous time in English football with Blackburn Rovers, for whom he made 356 of his 653 club appearances

BBC Radio Shropshire sports editor Nick Southall

For years, Shrewsbury Town supporters have awaited certainty over the club's future. Now, they have it.

After 30 years at the helm, Roland Wycherley's reign is over - the Football League's longest-serving owner.

The 85-year-old is credited by many with saving Shrewsbury when an ageing, flood-prone Gay Meadow was becoming an increasing burden on finances.

During his stewardship came some of the most memorable moments in the club's history: the Great Escape at Exeter, Jimmy Quinn's side winning promotion back to the Football League at the first attempt, Graham Turner's fairytale return, another promotion and then a League One Wembley play-off final under Paul Hurst.

Perhaps Wycherley's greatest achievement was overseeing the emotional move from the much-loved Meadow to Oteley Road, securing Town's long-term future.

For many years, the club earned a reputation as one of the best-run in the EFL, operating sustainably, avoiding the financial crises that have engulfed so many others.

Yet football has changed dramatically. Revenues have grown, investor-backed clubs have become increasingly common and Town find it harder to compete financially. While stability remained a strength, supporters increasingly questioned whether the club had reached its limits.

Wycherley's biggest footballing regret may be the missed opportunity to reach the Championship.

Hurst's side came agonisingly close in 2018, only to suffer Wembley heartbreak against Rotherham and miss a return to the second tier for the first time since the 1980s. Likewise, Steve Cotterill's side knocked on the door in 2022-23 but injuries at the tail-end of the season ultimately scuppered his chances.

Many Town supporters have only ever known Wycherley as owner. Now a new chapter begins as Davidson arrives with a track record of success in Scottish football, while Friedel brings both profile and experience from the game's highest levels.

Their arrival raises expectations. Can fresh investment improve recruitment, infrastructure and long-term ambitions? Could Shrewsbury become a success story in the next decade?

"Shrewsbury Town is a special club with a unique place in the landscape - and we believe it has limitless potential.

"We have put together a world-class investment team of business, legal, finance and sports professionals to help guide us and support our growth.

"Paired with the outstanding staff and leadership team that is already in place, our goal is to provide the community and our supporters with a club of which we can all be proud."

"It has been an honour and a privilege to serve as chairman and custodian of my boyhood football club, which I have proudly supported since the age of seven.

"My journey began by sponsoring an advertising board behind the Tech End goalmouth, before becoming an associate director in 1994, vice-chairman and, in 1996, chairman.

"One of the proudest moments was securing the move to our purpose-built stadium in 2007, bringing an end to 97 memorable years at the much-loved Gay Meadow. I firmly believe that move provided the club with a platform to progress.

"The club needs new investment to build on the foundations already in place, particularly the excellent work being undertaken within our foundation and also our academy."

#905. Grand Slam of Darts 2026: Littler alongside Greaves in mouth-watering Group A

Luke Littler has been drawn in Group A alongside Beau Greaves and Niels Zonneveld at the Grand Slam of Darts 2026; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The draw for the Grand Slam of Darts 2026 has taken place with Luke Littler grouped alongside Beau Greaves and Niels Zonneveld to make a mouth-watering Group A.

Littler and Greaves have faced each other twice before, with each young star picking up a victory and they will once again face-off in the evening session on Saturday November 14.

The world No 1 and two-time defending champion in Wolverhampton beat Greaves 6-5 in a deciding-leg at Players Championship 24 back in August.

Greaves beat Littler in a 6-5 thriller to clinch a spot in the World Youth Championship final in 2025.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Zonneveld and Littler played each other earlier this year, with the former securing a 6-5 win in the quarter-finals of the European Tour in March. Meanwhile, Greaves beat Zonneveld 6-3 in their meeting in Players Championship 31.

Luke Humphries, the 2023 winner, will take on Joe Cullen and Paolo Nebrida, while Group K catches the eye as James Wade faces Ricky Evans and Cam Crabtree.

Lisa Ashton is in Group B alongside Jermaine Wattimena and Alan Soutar, with Josh Rock in Group C with Kevin Doets and Tommy Morris, who surprisingly won Players Championship 34 recently.

#904. Michael Douglas’ Kids Dylan & Carys Support Him During Rare Appearance

Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones' kids Dylan Douglas, 26, and Carys Douglas, 23, helped honor their dad at the Art of Freedom Gala 2026 in New York City Nov. 4.

Michael Douglas was no solitary man during his latest outing.

The Basic Instinct actor was supported by his son Dylan, 26, and daughter Carys, 23—who he shares with wife Catherine Zeta-Jones—as he was honored at the Art of Freedom Gala 2026 Nov. 4.

Michael received a Lifetime Achievement Award by the Tibet House US at the event in New York, honoring his decades of peace activism and longtime role as a United Nations Messenger of Peace, a role he's held since 1998.

The 82-year-old sported a navy suit, posing alongside Dylan, who opted for a walnut-colored suit over a patterned shirt, and Carys, who wore a long-sleeved black top tucked into a tea-length khaki skirt adorned with an irregular pattern of sequins for the occasion.

After the event, Michael—who also shares son Cameron, 47, with ex-wife Diandra Luker—shared a photo of himself posing with his youngest children at the event.

"A wonderful night in NYC with @carys.douglas and @dylan__douglas," he wrote on Instagram. "Thank you to @tibethouse.us for honoring me with the Art of Freedom Award. Truly grateful for this special recognition and for such a memorable evening!"

And while Catherine wasn't able to attend the gala, their family's outing comes after the Wednesday actress recently opened up about what has made her and Michael's 26-year marriage last.

“Being kind to each other,” she told E! News last month. “And we have a very similar, sick, dry sense of humor. Which, in any circumstance that you find yourself in, within 28 years—we were two years together before we go married—you’ve got to find humor in it. It may not be funny at the time, but you got to look back at it and go, ‘You gotta laugh at that now, remember when that happened?’”

In addition to patience, the 57-year-old also cited giving one another “free reign” to pursue projects that appeal to them as a key to making their relationship work.

“He loves nothing more than when he sees the joy my acting brings me,” Catherine explained. “I don’t want to be away from him for seven months, coming back and forth, but we make it work. We always find those times and those long weekends where we can reconnect, and then off we go.”

Michael isn't the only star to step out with his kids lately. Keep reading for more about celebs and their mini-mes...

#903. A shock departure and key results - inside Wrexham's seismic week

Wrexham sit 15th in the Championship table after 15 matches of the 2026-27 season

In the midst of a pivotal week for Wrexham, the club announced a shock shake-up within the boardroom.

Gone was chief executive officer Michael Williamson, back came director Shaun Harvey as acting CEO.

While change occurred off the pitch, Phil Parkinson steadied the ship on it.

Watching over were co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac, who were in attendance for the 1-1 draw with Wolverhampton Wanderers, which came just shy of 24 hours after Williamson's exit.

Make no mistake, as Wrexham bid to achieve more success under their star owners, there is no doubt that recent changes at the Racecourse Ground have been immensely significant.

Wrexham toured in America in 2023, 2024 and 2026

From afar, Williamson's exit came as a surprise.

Williamson was appointed to the role of CEO just 34 days after Wrexham sealed promotion - at the time their second under Parkinson - into League One by thumping Forest Green Rovers 6-0 in north Wales.

The American - who previously worked at clubs including Inter Milan, DC United and Miami FC - oversaw huge growth as Wrexham evolved during their rise.

Overall staff numbers increased from 255 to 313 in his first year at the club, while Wrexham's iconic Racecourse Ground is also expanding.

Williamson had been a key figure in the development of Wrexham's new Â£69m Kop Stand, which is due to be completed next year.

He oversaw what was Wrexham's third successive promotion into the Championship - where the Red Dragons earned a highest-ever finish of seventh in 2025-26.

In November 2025, Williamson was named Football Industry Leader of the Year at the inaugural Global Football Industry Awards.

The club lauded Williamson for his pivotal role in the creation of the new academy facility at Darland High School, along with the subsequent approval of their English Football League (EFL) academy category three license.

The finances have continued to be boosted too.

Wrexham are expected to report a turnover of between Â£46m and Â£50m for the year ending June 2026, a huge jump on the Â£33.3m club record posted for their 2024-25 League One season, Williamson's first in north Wales.

But there has been growing discontent behind-the-scenes of late.

Wrexham claim point against in-form Wolves

Wrexham owners' presence uplifting - Parkinson

Wrexham made a key alteration to their transfer set-up in the summer.

Williamson took a prominent role in the club's transfer operations as director Harvey stepped down from day-to-day operations in early July.

Earlier this season, former Newcastle United chief Steve Nickson was appointed to the newly-created role of sporting director, a move welcomed by boss Parkinson. That said, he did not begin the role until after the summer window.

The transfer market proved difficult, as evidenced by the fact Wrexham were the last of the 24 Championship clubs to make a signing in the summer.

Two of their seven senior recruits - Callum O'Hare and Joe Worrall - joined on deadline day.

Only Danny Imray and Ben Whiteman arrived prior to the season opener against Middlesbrough in the League Cup on 7 August.

They were recently the subject of a bombshell announcement from the EFL regarding the registrations of summer signings O'Hare and Issa Kabore.

The club was fined Â£75,000 - of which Â£25,000 was suspended - after the EFL ruled that Kabore and O'Hare were ineligible to feature against Birmingham City and Millwall respectively earlier this season.

It led to the embarrassing situation of Southampton - who Wrexham mocked in the aftermath of the Spygate scandal - poking fun at the Red Dragons when they announced their line-up for the Sheffield United fixture in late October.

It was a game Wrexham went on to lose 1-0 following a lacklustre display, which led to Parkinson raising concerns over the performance of his players.

In the aftermath of the debacle, it was made clear the club want to recruit a new secretary - a vacancy that has existed since current club historian Geraint Parry stepped down from the role a year ago.

But the issues weren't simply behind-the-scenes. There have also been some concerns that the club has shown signs of losing its connection with supporters.

Changes to ticket policies in addition to the Â£10 surcharge - which was later scrapped due to a backlash from fans - required for supporters to use the Fanzone behind the temporary Kop stand in Williamson's first season at the club left the Wrexham faithful angered.

The club were also criticised in the summer for advertising merchandise featuring a white dragon, typically associated with England as opposed to the red dragon that features on the national flag of Wales.

It was seen as further evidence that the club's strong bond with those who have followed Wrexham through thick and thin has waned.

One beloved figure connected to the Red Dragons even told BBC Sport Wales that the achievements of some of the key members involved in Wrexham's rise have not been sufficiently recognised by some at the club.

Parkinson 'pleased' with point against Wolves

In a 139-word statement issued by Mac and Reynolds announcing Williamson's exit, the Hollywood pair wrote: "We remain focused on our most important task: to make the Wrexham community proud."

The word community was twice used in the brief statement. Plenty have made their own interpretations of the words chosen.

The announcement undoubtedly came out of the blue, with many staff on the ground in Wrexham only being made aware of the news shortly before the club's official announcement.

Parkinson himself was only informed on Friday morning prior to his pre-Wolves press conference, held at the club's Colliers Park training ground in the afternoon.

It was perhaps telling that Williamson's usual notes to fans were included in the Wolves matchday programme, despite his exit from the club a day earlier.

Only three days earlier, ahead of an impressive 2-0 victory against Middlesbrough, Williamson had utilised his programme notes to address the fiasco of Wrexham's breaches of player eligibility rules, incidents that occurred prior to sporting director Nickson's arrival.

"We co-operated with the EFL, carried out an internal review and have already taken steps to strengthen our processes and help prevent a recurrence," he wrote.

"As Wrexham AFC grows, our operations and infrastructure must keep pace with our ambitions on the pitch.

"Growth brings responsibility. We are proud of the progress being made, but we must be open and accountable when we fall short of our own standards. That is how we learn and build a stronger club for the long term."

Wrexham have largely operated in an efficient but ruthless fashion since being taken over by Reynolds and Mac in February 2021.

Icons including Paul Mullin, Elliot Lee, Andy Cannon, James McClean, Steven Fletcher and Ollie Palmer have all been moved on during the club's surge up the football pyramid.

Parkinson himself has been the recipient of some criticism during various stages of his five-and-a-half year tenure as boss.

The experienced manager rewarded the faith shown in him this week as his side collected four points in fixtures against two sides in Wolves and Boro that will likely be automatic promotion contenders come the latter stages of the campaign.

Williamson has not been as fortunate, and some of the reaction to his departure spoke volumes.

Former players Mullin, Lee, Cannon and Anthony Forde, along with Humphrey Ker - who recently stepped down as a director after five years with the club - were among those who liked a BBC Sport Wales post confirming Williamson's exit.

When one fan commented that those likes "says it all", former England midfielder Rob Lee - father of ex-Wrexham midfielder Elliot Lee - responded: "Yes it does."

Wrexham's acting CEO Shaun Harvey (right) is a long-time advisor to co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac

In Harvey, Wrexham feel they have someone who is more than just a safe pair of hands.

The 56-year-old has extensive knowledge of both the Welsh club and the English football structure following previous roles with Leeds United and Bradford City. He was also chief executive of the EFL between 2013 and 2019.

It is a huge part of the reason he has acted as an advisor to Reynolds and Mac ever since the duo became involved in the club.

Following his side's draw with Wolves, Parkinson said: "I had a brief chat with Shaun Harvey this morning.

"Shaun is back in a more official capacity, but he's always been around, he's been here since day one.

"He's an important figure. He understands everything about the club because he was one of the key people in starting off this journey with the owners."

There is clearly a strong bond between those at Wrexham and Harvey.

In the second minute of the contest with Wolves, Harvey headed to his seat in the Racecourse Ground's Macron Stand, known as the Mold Road Stand - the same stand in which Reynolds and Mac are situated for home games - and was roundly applauded by home fans.

The hope is that supporters will be continue to be applauding over the remaining months of the campaign.

Latest Wrexham news, analysis and fan views

Mac and Reynolds themselves stated Harvey has been an "integral part" of the club's journey.

Harvey could potentially land the role on a permanent basis, although an appointment would require approval from the Independent Football Regulator.

Nevertheless, it proved to be a seismic week for Wrexham.

The two-week international window will give those at the club a chance to take stock.

But the Championship grind will soon kick back in as Wrexham aim to build on their encouraging week on the field and continue their quest to clinch a play-off spot in just shy of six months' time.

"There's togetherness in the stands and with the boys on the pitch - but more than anything, there's just something about this place," the Deadpool star wrote on Instagram after the Wolves draw.

"Some of the best days of my life have been spent in this stadium, standing next to Rob Mac. Today was one of them. Up the Town."

#902. Diego Gómez hits another stunner as Brighton beat 10-man Brentford to go second

Who can stop Brighton’s ­ascension in English and European football? They are setting standards, ­practices ­leaving almost everybody else ­trailing in their wake. A ­second‑place position in the ­Premier League would once have read like a glitch in a ­Football ­Manager ­session. Not in November 2026, where they appear the only team capable of throwing down any sort of challenge to Arsenal.

Under low winter sun, Brentford, an opposition to which Brighton are often, if lazily, compared, were ­swatted aside. If Keith Andrews’s team, and their fans at the Amex ­Stadium, could level blame at a couple of ­refereeing decisions, they received little chance of rescuing anything. Brighton squeezed them, toyed with them.

If Pascal Gross, scorer of a perfectly hit penalty, attempted to dampen expectations of a title challenge, his manager, Fabian Hürzeler, allowed fans to dream. “They should always be excited, it’s our job to make them excited,” he said.

A successful return to the Amex Stadium following five Brighton away trips, more than 5,000 miles on the road including victories at ­Manchester City and Getafe over the past two outings. Brentford returned to a stadium where they have never won in the Premier League. Normal service was duly resumed, any Brighton negatives coming in a failure to add to their first-half goals.

An up-and-under straight from the kick-off was a rare Brentford foray into the Brighton box. Bart Verburggen catching it on the full prefaced an easy afternoon for the Brighton goalkeeper. There are many further dimensions to ­Hürzeler’s team. Last week Paul Scholes, an unlikely ­progressive, declared himself an admirer of a “level of ­coaching” he suggested is ­unsurpassed in ­English football. “The one thing that is non‑negotiable is to always put the team first,” Hürzeler said.

Diego Gómez’s opener was not as spectacular as the halfway-line goal of the season against Crystal Palace but a beauty nonetheless. Caressing the ball first with his left and then with his right, he laid up a thrash past Caoimhín Kelleher. Its trajectory was unerring, unstoppable. Hürzeler revealed: “Yesterday, he changed to shooting with [his] left foot … I couldn’t see him scoring with his left foot. I asked him after where this quality came from.”

The path to a commanding win opened up. Igor Thiago did not last many ­minutes beyond his failed attempt to lob ­Verburggen. Scuffling in midfield with Chema Andrés, his shove was first ruled a yellow by the referee, Michael Oliver. In stepped the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell: “violent conduct” and “with force” was the verdict from Stockley Park.

Afterwards, Andrews was ­visibly unhappy: “We’ve lost two games and both when down to 10 men. So we need to analyse ourselves first. In both scenarios we can do better. In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation.”

Infact, both Yehor Yarmolyuk and Vitaly Janelt were dismissed against Liverpool, and if Andrews rues such lapses of discipline he was more unhappy at the initial decision’s video-assisted overturn: “The game is in a state now of a place I don’t particularly like.”

Straying beyond the confines of his technical area in a manner likely to add him to Mikel Arteta’s “massive storage of images” of such breaches, Andrews asked his team to dig deep but Brighton’s dominance of possession became near-total.

Luka Vuskovic, ­serving ­previously as a deep-lying playmaker, won the penalty. Keane Lewis-Potter’s ­panicked response to a physical 18-yard box mismatch was to snatch at the ­Croatian’s shirt. Gross’s penalty was struck as truly as Gómez’s goal. “We need to be cuter,” Andrews said. “I take real pride in the way we defend set pieces and we need to do better because that wasn’t good.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andrews’s half-time ­adjustments, bringing on Yarmolyuk and Nathan Collins, was an attempt to protect Brentford’s goal difference. Brighton continued to pile on pressure, their ­possession share reaching beyond 75%. A set piece became Brentford’s sole route back, though Mathias Jensen’s diagonal into ­Verbruggen’s hands would not have passed muster in rugby’s Nations Championship.

Ironic cheers from the away end came when Brentford won a corner, and then another – rare excitement at Brighton’s defenders being asked to do something other than build an attack. The visitors’ fighting spirit at least sustained, though threatened to spill over. When Kevin Schade shoved ­Vuskovic to the ground by the touchline, another red card was a possibility, only for Oliver and Attwell to rule a yellow as sufficient this time.

Brighton’s push for honours and further horizons will require more than spectacular goals. “You see the Premier League, the margins, you look at the results – we are not ­getting carried away yet,” Gross said. “Every game we have to suffer a lot.”

Hürzeler, like Andrews constantly straying beyond the confines of his technical area, does not countenance any let-ups. When Brighton meet the unstinting demands of their coach, so many are left in their wing mirrors.

#900. NWSL playoffs scheduling snafu: Washington Spirit keep Audi Field; Gotham move to Icahn

Washington to play in Saturday noon broadcast window

Shift to Northwest Stadium was reportedly in play

Gotham move to Icahn amid ‘atrocious’ pitch conditions

The Washington Spirit will play their NWSL semi-final at Audi Field after the club reached a deal to avoid playing a playoff game at Northwest Stadium, home of the NFL’s Washington Commanders. Top-seeded Gotham FC, meanwhile, will play their game at the 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium on Randall’s Island in New York City because of poor pitch quality at Sports Illustrated Stadium, their usual home.

The Spirit will play their semi-final against the Utah Royals on 14 November (Saturday) at noon, while Gotham FC will host the Kansas City Current on Sunday at 3pm.

The NWSL has had to maneuver through significant venue-availability conflicts in the past few days, balancing two sought-after national television broadcast windows with issues at the stadiums of the semi-finalists with home field advantage. Many of the teams in the league are not the primary tenants or owners of their stadium, meaning they are not able to exert full control or say over scheduling or conditions.

Audi Field has been the Spirit’s full-time home since 2023, and it has hosted raucous crowds for the team’s playoff runs, including Sunday’s 4-1 win over the Portland Thorns to advance to the semi-final.

However, a Division III college football game between the Coast Guard Academy and the Merchant Marine Academy was scheduled to be played at Audi Field on Saturday afternoon, a national TV window that the league would not be willing or able to move.

ESPN reported earlier this week that the NWSL had been preparing scenarios that would see the Spirit play their playoff game on Saturday at Northwest Stadium, a 64,000-seat venue in Landover, Maryland, roughly 10 miles north-east of downtown Washington where the team have never played a game in their 14-year existence, in the event that both the Spirit and top-seeded Gotham advanced to the semi-finals.

The Spirit are not the primary tenants at Audi Field. The stadium is owned and operated by MLS team DC United. The Spirit would not confirm if the college football game has been moved to a different location or date. As of Monday afternoon, it was still listed for its original time of 1pm on Saturday on both schools’ websites.

The location of Gotham’s semi-final against Kansas City was announced Monday afternoon. Though Sports Illustrated Stadium was available for the Sunday slot, the primary cause for concern was the state of the pitch. It has taken much wear-and-tear after hosting soccer and rugby matches in recent weeks, and would have hosted the semi-final just one day after MLS’s New York Red Bulls, the stadium’s owners, play a friendly against Liga MX side Club América.

During Gotham’s 1-0 win over Seattle in their quarter-final on Sunday afternoon, the venue’s field was patchy and sandy, with many visible brown spots. Reign captain Jess Fishlock described the field as “atrocious”. Gotham coach Juan Carlos Amoros apologized for the conditions and said the club attempted to mitigate the circumstances without success.

“Let’s be real, there’s no way a playoff game should be played on that shit,” Reign head coach Laura Harvey told ESPN. “I just can’t believe they’ve allowed it. They knew it last week.”

The league reportedly fined Gotham $10,000 for the poor conditions in their regular-season finale game on 4 November.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth. What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league or our fans deserve,” Gotham captain Tierna Davidson said in the club’s news release about the game relocation.

Icahn Stadium mostly hosts track events and is not well-trafficked, but has a natural grass pitch funded by MLS club New York Cit FC in 2024. It has hosted Gotham games in the past, including a regular-season match in July. Its capacity, though, is just less than half of Gotham FC’s average attendance this season.

“This was an extremely difficult decision, and one we did not take lightly,” said Yael Averbuch West, the president of soccer operations for Gotham FC, said in a statement. “After thoughtful consultation with coach Juan Carlos Amorós, our team captains and our ownership, we felt it was important to prioritize a playing surface that appropriately allows our athletes to perform at their best.

We fully understand and appreciate the impact this has on our fans, and we are equally disappointed that we won’t have the opportunity to play in front of more of our supporters at our home stadium. Unfortunately, we were faced with a difficult situation, and at the end of the day, the game is played on the field.”
