#808. COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Delegates arriving at the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya for 12 days of talks.Credit: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock

The United Nations annual climate meeting starting today is the first to take place after confirmation that global warming will overshoot the headline limit of 1.5 °C. The aim of keeping warming within 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures was set out in the 2015 Paris agreement.

As tens of thousands of delegates and observers arrive in Antalya, Turkey, for the COP31 meeting, some scientists and climate advocates say the 12-day event must discuss how to deal with the overshoot. Along with cutting emissions, this includes practical ways of removing massive volumes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

The UN Environment Programme last month acknowledged that, under all plausible emissions trajectories, the world will surpass the 1.5 °C target agreed at COP21 in Paris. Its Limiting Overshoot report is the first UN report to state explicitly that overshoot is now inevitable. It also laid out how to bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C target this century.

In addition to slashing emissions to near-zero levels, the report confirmed the need to remove hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 from the atmosphere this century, either using CO2 removal technologies or nature-based approaches such as reforestation. “[K]eeping 1.5 °C within reach requires climate policy to evolve to include the removal of already emitted [greenhouse gases],” the report states.

This idea to limit the “magnitude and the duration” of overshooting 1.5 °C is expected to shape discussion among parties at the COP meeting, says Clea Schumer, a research associate at the World Resources Institute, an environmental research and advocacy organization in Washington DC. Some language on limiting overshoot was included in the final decision of the COP30 summit last year in Belém, Brazil, but CO2 removal has mostly gone unmentioned.

Most governments “are happy that they finally don’t have to pretend any more that we will make it” to 1.5 °C, says Oliver Geden, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin. They now want to limit overshoot, “but how we actually do that, nobody is talking about”, he adds.

Steve Smith, a climate researcher at the University of Oxford, UK, agrees. CO2 removal has sparked controversy in the past over concerns that it might distract from the need to cut emissions. But it is possible that CO2 removal could move up the agenda amid discussions about the necessary return from overshoot, he says.

Environmental advocacy groups, such as New York-based Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), that had been skeptical of CO2 removal, have now changed their position. A report from the organisation in September called on environmentalists to support CO2 removal in the same way they supported renewable energy and electrification.

"It is now time to set the stage for another—an industry that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere—to contribute to the fight for climate stability," the report says

However, so far, no country has included clearly quantified CO2 removal targets in climate commitments submitted to the UN, says Smith. Such targets would be necessary to achieve the large scales of CO2 removal that could bring warming back below 1.5 °C. “We really want governments to cut emissions and set out clear plans for scaling up CO2 removal," says Smith

Some scientists say the failure to cut emissions fast enough to avoid overshoot is a sign that there need to be reforms to COP meetings.

“We need to first recognize that global policy has failed. This is a moment of self-critique,” says Johan Rockström, a climate scientist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany.

Rockström leads a group of scientists advising a coalition of around 60 countries working in parallel to the COP. The coalition wants the world to move faster to transition away from fossil fuels, and met for the first time in April in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Rockström, together with other prominent climate scientists and diplomats, has argued for some years that the COP process needs reform. Ahead of COP31, he told Nature that a top priority should be to allow for decisions to be made by majority votes among parties. Currently, agreements must involve all countries coming to a consensus. In the past, this has meant that a small number of states can block decisions backed by the majority. “Overshoot gives even more impetus for the need for reform. It shows that we’ve not been able to make the progress that we need,” says Rockström.

However, that doesn’t mean COP meetings don’t still have an important role, say climate advocates. “COP gatherings have had a massive impact,” says Yamide Dagnet, a senior vice-president in Washington DC at the NRDC. “But their success has increasingly been measured in degrees averted,” she adds.

When the Paris agreement was signed in 2015, the world looked likely to reach around 4 °C of warming this century. Under current policies, the UN Emissions Gap report found that has declined to between 2.6 and 2.8 °C of warming this century, with a small chance of reaching significantly hotter temperatures.

Climate researchers say it is unrealistic to expect the COP meetings to shift the trajectory of the world’s countries on their own. “Action, in the end, has to be national,” says Ed Carr, senior scientist at the Boston, Massachusetts, office of the Stockholm Environment Institute, a non-profit research organization.

#806. Why Guitarricadelafuente Said Yes to La Bola Negra Without a Script

Guitarricadelafuente explained the unconventional way he was cast in La Bola Negra and the emotions he felt writing the film’s original song “La Nieve.”

For Guitarricadelafuente, La Bola Negra was definitely his jam.

The Spanish singer-songwriter revealed how he went from making music to making movie magic in the drama, which is already an awards season frontrunner.

“The truth is that I said yes to this role a bit blindly because the script wasn't written yet,” Guitarricadelafuente told E! News in an exclusive interview, translated from Spanish, at the 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala Nov. 7. “There was only the idea of the character of Sebastián and for me it was like a gift from heaven to be able to participate in this film.”

Plus, the 29-year-old (real name Álvaro Lafuente Calvo) had good reason to trust his instincts. After all, he was already a longtime fan of the film’s co-writers and co-directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as “Los Javis.”

“They knew they could count on me without me having the story in mind—they already knew I could do it,” he shared. “It was something that made me immediately say yes.”

Acting wasn’t the only way Guitarricadelafuente got to flex his creative muscles. He also wrote the original song “La Nieve” for the movie, though he admitted he “didn’t know where to begin.”

Ultimately, he found inspiration in the film’s focus on poet Federico García Lorca.

“The truth is that it was a beautiful journey to be inspired by all that poetry of Lorca that is so present throughout the film,” he explained, “and something to pay homage to all those lives that could not be possible in some way.”

Bringing Sebastián to life helped him find his voice, too.

“It came out as if I were able to experience the character in my own flesh,” he added, “and for all of that to come out in the most honest way possible.”

La Bola Negra lands on Netflix Dec. 2. Read on to see the other movies hitting screens soon.

#805. Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The results challenge a long-standing assumption about the enormous forces needed to create such an extreme substance. They also offer scientists a new way to investigate the conditions that prevailed during the universe's earliest moments.

Quark–gluon plasma (QGP) is an unusual state of matter that appears under tremendous pressure and heat. At temperatures exceeding 100,000 times those at the Sun's center, particles such as protons and neutrons can no longer maintain their normal structure. Instead, they break apart into quarks and the gluons that ordinarily bind them together.

Physicists believe that this was the state of matter throughout the universe during the first millionths of a second after the Big Bang. Nearly 14 billion years later, researchers can briefly recreate these extraordinary conditions by smashing atomic nuclei together at extremely high energies inside the LHC.

For decades, scientists believed that generating this plasma required collisions involving very heavy atomic nuclei, particularly lead. Lead nuclei are more than 200 times heavier than the protons typically used in LHC experiments, making them capable of producing the intense conditions thought necessary for QGP to form.

However, recent discoveries have increasingly called that assumption into question.

Earlier this year, the ALICE collaboration, which specializes in studying quark–gluon plasma, identified another indication of QGP formation in proton–proton and proton–lead collisions. The previous year, LHC researchers had also reported the first hints of this plasma emerging from oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Now, more detailed investigations have revealed multiple signs that QGP can form in collisions involving both oxygen and neon nuclei, providing stronger evidence that the conditions required to create this primordial matter are not limited to heavy atomic collisions.

One of the clearest ways to identify quark–gluon plasma is to examine what happens when energetic quarks and gluons travel through it.

As these particles move through the extremely hot and dense material, they lose some of their energy. Scientists call this process parton energy loss, and it provides an important clue that QGP has formed.

The ATLAS collaboration clearly detected this effect by studying pairs of particle jets generated during oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions. These jets are concentrated streams of particles produced when energetic quarks and gluons emerge from a collision.

Researchers observed differences in energy between the paired jets, indicating that some of the particles had lost energy while traveling through the surrounding material.

The effect was especially pronounced during more direct, head-on (central) collisions. Such impacts are expected to create a larger volume of plasma, giving particles more material to travel through and causing greater energy loss.

Preliminary ATLAS results provide additional support for this interpretation. By examining charged particles that recoil in the opposite direction from photons, researchers found a similar relationship between energy loss and how centrally the nuclei collided.

The ALICE, CMS, and LHCb collaborations searched for the same underlying process using a different approach. Rather than focusing primarily on the energy of particle jets, they examined how the plasma appears to reduce the production of certain energetic particles.

CMS found that charged-particle production was suppressed in both oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions compared with proton–proton collisions. This reduction is consistent with particles losing energy inside quark–gluon plasma and provides further evidence that the exotic material can form in collisions involving lighter nuclei.

LHCb reported another important clue in a separate study. The collaboration investigated particles containing a charm quark and a lighter quark, comparing how strongly their production was suppressed in oxygen and neon collisions.

The suppression was more pronounced in the heavier neon collisions. That is precisely the kind of behavior scientists would expect if larger collisions produce greater volumes of plasma, causing particles to lose more energy as they pass through it.

However, reduced particle production does not necessarily prove that energy loss is responsible. Other physical processes could potentially produce similar effects.

To investigate this possibility, ALICE compared the production of neutral pions, another type of subatomic particle, in oxygen–oxygen and proton–oxygen collisions.

The comparison provided unambiguous evidence of parton energy loss in oxygen–oxygen collisions, strengthening the case that even relatively small nuclear collisions can generate conditions associated with quark–gluon plasma.

Researchers also looked for another distinctive signature of QGP involving particles made from a heavy quark and its corresponding antiquark.

These pairs can briefly bind together following high-energy collisions. Some are more tightly bound than others, making them differently susceptible to disruption by the surrounding plasma.

By examining which bound states are suppressed and by how much, physicists can gather additional evidence about whether QGP is present.

The CMS collaboration found evidence of this varying suppression in particles called upsilon mesons, which consist of a bottom quark paired with its antiquark. The researchers identified the effect by comparing oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions.

LHCb also reported preliminary evidence of similar behavior, this time using data from proton–oxygen and oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Together, these observations add another piece to the growing body of evidence that primordial plasma can emerge in nuclear collisions much smaller than those traditionally used to study it.

The ALICE collaboration has identified yet another possible signature of quark–gluon plasma, this time involving the directions in which particles travel after a collision.

In preliminary findings, researchers observed that particles containing three quarks (baryons) showed a stronger preference for certain directions than particles composed of two quarks (mesons) during oxygen–oxygen collisions.

This behavior is known as anisotropic flow. Rather than spreading evenly in every direction, particles emerge in patterns influenced by the conditions inside the material created during the collision.

The leading explanation involves the formation of QGP. When particles with intermediate momenta emerge from this plasma, they can inherit collective motion from the quarks that make them up.

Because baryons contain three quarks while mesons contain only two, baryons can inherit more of this flow, producing the difference observed in the experiment.

This distinctive pattern provides another potential indication that the extreme matter of the early universe is being recreated in oxygen collisions.

Scientists are continuing to analyze data from collisions involving lighter atomic nuclei, searching for additional evidence of how quark–gluon plasma forms and behaves.

The findings are reshaping the understanding of the conditions needed to produce one of the most extreme states of matter known to physics. What once appeared to require collisions between massive nuclei can now be investigated through much smaller systems, giving researchers new opportunities to explore the behavior of matter under extraordinary conditions.

Meanwhile, CERN is upgrading the Large Hadron Collider into the more powerful High-Luminosity LHC. The enhanced accelerator will allow scientists to collect substantially more collision data and investigate the properties of quark–gluon plasma in greater detail.

With each new discovery, researchers are gaining a clearer picture of the remarkable state of matter that dominated the universe during its first fleeting moments after the Big Bang.

After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection.

Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it.

"The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said. "It's to do something that only 651 people have been able to do: miss Earth and miss other Earthlings."

Glover was one of the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. Alongside NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them.

As the Orion spacecraft traversed the far side of the moon, the Artemis II crew watched Earth disappear below the lunar horizon before losing radio contact with our planet. Around 40 minutes later, Earth came back into view as the spacecraft emerged from behind the moon.

For Glover, however, the experience was about much more than the view. He believes that if everyone on Earth had the opportunity to make the same journey, they would come away with a similar appreciation for what they'd left behind.

"I think all of us would say something in our native language, in the most basic way we can communicate about love, joy, hope and inspiration," Glover said.

Although Glover shared the extraordinary journey with three fellow astronauts, the four of them were separated from the rest of humanity by hundreds of thousands of miles.

And for Glover, that distance brought with it a strange contradiction: the farther he traveled from humanity, the more he longed to connect with it."At the point of ultimate disconnection, [there is] this longing for connection," Glover said.

The experience gave him a perspective that he carried back into everyday life.

"There are moments where I am rushing through traffic and want to get where I'm going because I'm being selfish," Glover admitted. "But I don't have to stay there."

Instead, he remembers what it felt like to look back at a planet so distant that everyone who has ever lived could be covered by his hand.

"I wish you could all feel what it's like to come back home after that disconnection," he said.

Astronauts often describe experiencing the "overview effect", a profound shift in perspective that can come from seeing Earth from space. But Glover believes that there's something equally powerful waiting to be discovered much closer to home.

When asked by a Starmus VIII attendee whether people needed to undergo something extraordinary to develop a greater sense of kindness toward others, his answer was no.

Glover encouraged people to look more closely at the natural world around them, whether that meant walking along the beach, watching the ocean or simply examining a leaf held up to sunlight. Even something as ordinary as a leaf, he explained, is capable of turning sunlight into food through photosynthesis. And although science can explain how that happens, understanding the process doesn't make it any less remarkable.

"We have to choose to be moved by these things," Glover said.

He worries that modern life, with its endless technological distractions, has made it all too easy to overlook the extraordinary things happening around us.

"Familiarity breeds contempt. Have you heard this? I think it's worse than that. Familiarity breeds indifference," he said.

Glover has a name for this perspective he hopes people can rediscover without traveling into space: The sea level effect.

It's about finding the same sense of wonder and connection that astronauts experience in orbit, but right here on Earth, where most of us spend our lives. And ultimately, Glover believes the greatest wonder isn't the moon, the stars, or even the incredible complexity of nature. It's the people we share our planet with.

"I think the hardest place to see this miracle is in the actual greatest miracle in the universe: other humans," he said.

"We all feel it with babies, but when we get old enough to have opinions, we start to want to argue with each other."

Glover hopes that by taking the time to appreciate the natural world, people might become a little more willing to appreciate one another too.

"That's the mission that I want to be part of for the rest of my life," Glover said.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#802. Incident-by-incident: Was it a bad weekend for VAR?

Manchester United's last-gasp equaliser against Aston Villa survived a VAR review for a potential foul

Whisper it quietly, but the statistics say video assistant referee decisions have been pretty good in the Premier League so far this season.

The Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel, which looks at every contentious decision and votes whether it is right or wrong, reported just two VAR errors after eight rounds of matches.

At the same stage last season, there had been six mistakes.

Then came this weekend, during which almost every top-flight game had a controversial decision.

BBC Sport looks at most of these situations - there really were too many to do them all - and assesses the likelihood that the KMI Panel will add to the list of errors.

Man Utd grab a point in dramatic fashion late on against Aston Villa

Incident 1: Penalty awarded to Manchester United for a foul by Boubacar Kamara on Matheus Cunha in the 16th minute.

Verdict: The spot-kick was awarded because the Villa defender went through Cunha to win the ball. Replays clearly showed the first contact was on the Brazilian's foot.

What the KMI Panel might say: This will be a correct decision.

Incident 2: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

Verdict : There are similarities to a goal Arsenal scored at Old Trafford last season, when William Saliba leant into United goalkeeper Altay BayÄ±ndÄ±r.

Lammens was not looking at the ball, which increases the chances of a VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel might say: With the higher bar for an intervention in the Premier League, and minimal contact, it is unlikely to be a VAR error to not disallow the goal.

Why Arsenal should have been given a penalty against Hull

Incident: Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor for a penalty, but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered this incident in detail on Saturday. As the foul happened before any potential offside offence, the penalty should have been awarded.

What the KMI Panel might say: Even though it feels wrong to reward a player in an offside position with a penalty, the law says otherwise and this is likely to be a mistake.

Should Bogle have seen red for this challenge in the Leeds v Tottenham game?

Incident: Jayden Bogle fouled Mathys Tel, with referee John Brooks giving the free-kick but no sanction for the Leeds player. The VAR, Tony Harrington, opted not to send Brooks to the monitor for a red card.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered the merits of this incident on Saturday. It was a difficult call for the VAR, because Bogle caused the foul with his supporting rather than his challenging foot. Still, it was a very painful challenge and some believe it should have been a red card.

What the KMI Panel might say: Was it an unfortunate incident, or a tackle which endangered the opponent? This will depend upon which former players are on the KMI Panel for this week, because it has split opinion among ex-pros.

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

All three incidents were covered in more detail by BBC Sport on Friday.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by James Tarkowski, but no penalty was awarded.

Verdict: While the interpretation on hair pulling was relaxed for this season, meaning this would not be a red card, there appeared to be a yank of the hair by the Everton defender.

What the KMI Panel might say: Incorrect decision, penalty kick.

Incident 2: Another penalty claim for Coventry as Everton's Vitalii Mykolenko clipped Taiwo Awoniyi on the edge of the box.

Verdict: Replays shows that the contact on Awoniyi was made just before the line.

What the KMI Panel might say: Correct decision, no penalty.

Incident 3: Thierno Barry put Everton in front in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

Verdict: The VAR determined there was no conclusive evidence for a handball, yet there does appear to be a deviation and the goal probably should have been ruled out.

What the KMI Panel might say: As the VAR does not have the super-zoom - this takes a few minutes to calibrate and is not available instantly - no VAR intervention might be supported. This was the case with a goal scored by Crystal Palace against Nottingham Forest. It could be a split vote.

Igor Thiago will be suspended for three Premier League games after his VAR red card for violent conduct

Incident: Igor Thiago was sent off following a VAR review after he caught the head of Chema Andres with his forearm.

Verdict: The Brentford striker can consider himself unfortunate, as there is doubt that he truly intended to catch the Spaniard in the face.

What the KMI Panel might say: It may seem like a soft dismissal, but the VAR intervention is likely to be supported because the law does say that a strike to the head should be a red card, unless force is negligible.

'Yellow card for me' - Dublin on Thiago red card

Incident: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio.

Verdict: We saw a similar incident the 2024-25 season when Arsenal defender William Saliba headed Joao Pedro after the Brighton striker had won the ball. This was voted to be a correct penalty decision.

What the KMI Panel might say: This incident is not quite the same as Saliba on Pedro, and more of a 50-50 clash. It may be voted as an on-field error, but not to the threshold for VAR.

Incident: Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge from both Luke O'Nien and Jules Ahoka, and asked for a penalty. Referee Jarred Gillett did not give a foul.

Verdict: A foul is determined by the first contact on the attacker. That a player falls into the box with contact continuing would not make it a penalty. Only on holding offences is continuing contact relevant.

What the KMI Panel might say: There is no conclusive evidence that any initial foul contact happened inside the area, so no penalty is likely to be supported.

Incident: Newcastle thought they had taken the lead at Craven Cottage, only for the goal to be ruled out for a foul by Yoane Wissa on Timothy Castagne.

Verdict: Matthias Jaissle was perplexed in his post-match interview, yet he would surely be furious if a Fulham player held one of his defenders back to create on onside corridor for another attacker to score.

What the KMI Panel might say: This is likely to be voted as a correct decision.

BBC Sport estimates that there are two decisions which the KMI Panel is very likely to log as a VAR error: not awarding penalties to Arsenal and Coventry.

Two further calls, Barry's goal and the potential red card to Bogle, may be errors but will depend who is on the panel and where their subjective opinion lies.

The others on the list are likely to be correct.

So we are potentially looking at two to four errors, which is not a good weekend.

#801. Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two

Black holes are known for merging when two of them collide, but could the reverse ever happen? Could a single black hole somehow divide into two smaller ones? A new theoretical study suggests that this extraordinary possibility may not be entirely ruled out by physics, although the conditions required would be extreme.

The research, published in Physical Review D under the title "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," examines the physical laws that keep black holes intact and whether certain circumstances could allow them to break apart.

"In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen," says Francesco Sannino, co-author of the study and a professor of physics at University of Naples Federico II in Italy and Quantum Field Theory Center at University of Southern Denmark.

The research team also included Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a researcher with the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint CNRS and Sorbonne Université laboratory in Paris. Additional contributors were Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Why Black Holes Normally Cannot Split Apart

One of the biggest obstacles to a black hole splitting comes from thermodynamics, the branch of physics that governs how energy behaves and how physical systems change.

A central concept is entropy, which describes how many different microscopic arrangements a system can have while appearing unchanged from the outside. Black holes have entropy, and this property places important limits on what can happen to them.

For a black hole that is not rotating, dividing into two smaller black holes would reduce the total entropy. Such a decrease makes the process thermodynamically unfavorable, helping explain why black holes do not ordinarily break apart.

However, the researchers found that the situation could change dramatically when a black hole spins at an exceptionally high speed.

Extreme Rotation Could Allow Black Holes to Split

The team's calculations suggest that rapid rotation may create a narrow opening in the physical rules that normally prevent black holes from dividing. In principle, a sufficiently fast spinning black hole could overcome the usual thermodynamic restriction.

But there is another major obstacle. Even if a black hole could divide, the two resulting objects would need to move far enough apart to avoid immediately merging again.

"But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," says Francesco Sannino.

The study's unusual title refers to the shape that a black hole's boundary would trace through space and time if such a split occurred. This boundary, called the horizon, would begin as a single structure before separating into two distinct branches.

Viewed across time, the resulting shape would resemble a pair of trousers, with one upper section dividing into two "legs." This is the idea behind the term "pair-of-pants topologies."

Extra Dimensions Offer Another Possibility

The researchers also investigated more unusual scenarios involving theories in which space has additional dimensions beyond the three we experience in everyday life.

Physicists have already identified objects resembling black holes in some of these theoretical models that can become unstable and start breaking apart. These possibilities suggest that the familiar rules governing black holes may not apply in the same way under more exotic conditions.

In certain cases, splitting could even become thermodynamically favorable, especially when one of the two resulting black holes is much smaller than the other.

However, a process being allowed or favored by thermodynamics does not necessarily mean it will happen. Researchers still need to determine whether such fragmentation can physically occur and what conditions would make it possible.

Could Astronomers Detect a Black Hole Splitting?

The scientists are now working to better understand how likely these events might be. The answer may depend on aspects of gravity that go beyond Einstein's theory, making the problem especially challenging.

"We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein's theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers," says Francesco Sannino.

Although there is currently no confirmed observation of a black hole splitting, the possibility of detecting signals from tiny fragments offers a potential way to investigate the idea. Such evidence could provide valuable clues about the behavior of gravity under some of the most extreme conditions in the universe.

Sannino is the director of the Quantum Field Theory Center (ℏQTC), which is affiliated with the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science (IMADA) at the University of Southern Denmark. He is also affiliated with the Danish Institute for Advanced Study and the Department of Physics "Ettore Pancini" at the University of Naples Federico II. In addition, he serves as a visiting professor at Durham University.

The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be a last of its kind.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists.

The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft.

The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong. However, NASA quickly fixed the problem and got Galileo working again.

Less than a year later, Galileo threw itself into Jupiter's atmosphere. The spacecraft was crushed by the high pressure in Jupiter's atmosphere, but its data still survives on Earth.

The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be the last time the probe would ever swing by one of Jupiter's moons.

While it may not look like it in Galileo's black and white images above and below, Amalthea is tinted red due sulfur contamination on its surface. The moon is small, about 168 miles long, and orbits about 112,468 miles (181,000 km) from Jupiter (much closer to the planet than the Earth and its moon).

Galileo flew within 99 miles of Amalthea during its flyby, which also marked the closest Galileo would get to Jupiter before its death dive in September 2005.

"Scientists studying data from NASA's Galileo spacecraft have found that Jupiter's moon Amalthea is a pile of icy rubble less dense than water," NASA announced in May 2005

"Amalthea is throwing us a curve ball," Torrence Johnson, a study co-author on the Almathea flyby and project scientist for the Galileo mission at JPL, said in 2005. "Its density is well below that of water ice, and even with substantial porosity, Amalthea probably contains a lot of water ice, as well as rock."

Originally known as Jupiter V (because it was the fifth Jupiter moon discovered after the so-called Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), Amalthea was named after naiad, or water nymph, from Greek mythology.

It is fitting that Amalthea was the last of Jupiter's moons to be visited by the Galileo spacecraft. The moon was also last Jupiter moon to be discovered by visual observations when it was first disovered by astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard in September 1892 using the Lick Observatory telescope in California.

The Galileo spacecraft ultimately crashed into Jupiter on Sept. 21, 2005, less than a year after its Amalthea flyby.

#798. Brady ends association with Birmingham City

Brady brought an end to his illustrious NFL career in 2023

NFL legend Tom Brady has ended his association with top-of-the-table Championship side Birmingham City.

The seven-time Super Bowl champion became a minority owner in the St Andrew's club in August 2023 when he "entered a partnership" with club owners Knighthead Capital Management LLC.

Part of Brady's role involved him being chairman of an advisory board at Birmingham, with the club saying he would be "both investing [as well as] committing his time and extensive expertise" following his arrival.

However, the Blues announced his exit, external with a statement headlined 'Tom Brady departure'.

They added: "Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.

"It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community."

Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six of his Super Bowl titles with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Following the end of his playing career, he also acquired a stake Las Vegas Raiders, while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.

On top of that, Brady's commitments also include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

He leaves with Birmingham top of the Championship on goal difference with 29 points after 15 games.

#797. IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos

An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.

Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.

Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.

Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.

Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.

"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"

Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything

Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.

Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.

The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.

"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."

How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos

The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).

Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."

For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."

The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.

Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos

During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.

His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.

These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.

By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.

IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.

When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.

For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.

"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."

Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang

The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.

Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.

Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.

Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.

"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

#796. People don't know full story behind England exile - White

Ben White made his first England appearance in more than three years against Uruguay in March

Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection - but says he would make the same decision again.

White, who has been named in Thomas Tuchel's squad for upcoming Nations League fixtures, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons.

He then made himself unavailable for selection for the rest of Gareth Southgate's reign, and was booed by some fans in March's 1-1 draw with Ukraine after returning to the squad under Tuchel.

Asked by BBC Radio 5 live's football correspondent John Murray what he would say to people who define his England career by what happened in Qatar, White said: "I think obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

"It's been amazing [though], obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it is amazing to be here now."

White is now 29 and asked if he would have done anything differently in hindsight, he added: "No, I don't think I would.

"Obviously, I was a bit younger, I am a bit older now.

"I think as a person I am quite real and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make.

"So, one that I am not happy about, but obviously it happened and [it is] time to move on."

White came on for his first England appearance since 2022 in March's 1-1 draw with Uruguay and was booed by some supporters before he scored but also gave away the penalty that led to the visitors' equaliser.

After that, Chelsea midfielder Jordan Henderson said he and his fellow England players would always support White, while Tuchel said recently that the defender deserves "a new chapter" and "positive feedback from the crowd".

Asked how he dealt with the emotions of that night at Wembley, White added: "Before the game I was thinking 'don't not stand out, but [take it] nice and easy'.

"Then I came on and obviously got booed, then I scored, then I gave away a penalty.

"So, it was obviously full of emotions that night, [but] it was a good night."

England play Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before taking on world champions Spain in Madrid three days later.

White is looking to add to his six England caps in this international break and said: "It is obviously an amazing privilege to be called up.

"The feeling is the same every time you do get this chance to play for England. It's one I am really looking forward to this week."

Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas.

The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29).

The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027.

Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun. QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.

According to the Minor Planet Center, the closest QQ8 will come to our planet during this stay is around 353,000 miles (568,000 kilometers). That is around 110,000 miles (177,000 km) further out than the average distance between Earth and the moon. Even if QQ8 were to come close enough to collide with Earth, it would likely be completely destroyed in our planet's atmosphere before it reaches the surface, as it is only around 6 feet (2 meters) in diameter.

This is far from the first time Earth has snagged itself a mini-moon, more accurately called a temporary satellite. In fact, research last year suggested that our planet could be orbited by as many as six mini-moons at any given time, with many of these being fragments of our more permanent natural satellite, the moon.

While QQ8 is tiny, it is larger than the average mini-moon. That is according to modelling earlier this year that suggested the average size for a temporary satellite is 75 centimeters (30 inches) across.

The same modelling suggested the average stay for such an object would be around nine months.

So if QQ8 was captured in April 2026, that means it should move away in January 2027.

The researchers behind those findings suggested that, were Earth to gravitationally grip a space rock around 10 feet (3 meters) wide, it could serve as a mini-moon for 10 to 20 years.

#794. NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice

Located in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, Vega Island has a particularly haunting appearance when viewed from above. Its rocky and icy features resemble a grinning skull seen from the side, seemingly gazing toward nearby Devil Island. But behind this unusual sight is a more serious story about the changing condition of Antarctica's glaciers.

NASA satellite images show the island during the beginning of Antarctic autumn and during spring. The images were captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.)

Several natural landmarks create the skull's distinctive appearance. A nunatak, which is a rocky peak rising above the surrounding ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge of material left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth. Meanwhile, Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms what looks like the skull's lower jaw.

The two satellite views also reveal a striking difference in snow coverage. In March 2025, snow blanketed the icy terrain, consistent with March being the wettest month in the region. By October 2026, however, extensive sections of the island were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the unusually large areas of exposed ice observed in October. According to Pelto, the exposed surfaces on Vega Island and neighboring islands suggest that relatively little fresh snow accumulated over the winter. Some of that snow was also lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds that swept snow away.

“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”

The lack of snow could have important consequences as Antarctica moves into its warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker, exposed ice absorbs more solar energy. As daylight increases and temperatures rise, these darker surfaces are likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up glacier melting.

Even a modest amount of new snowfall could temporarily slow that process by covering the exposed ice.

“Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said.

Continued melting could also gradually transform the island's unsettling appearance. The same ice and rock formations that give Vega Island its skull shape are vulnerable to changes as the glaciers retreat.

“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”

Scientists have been studying Vega Island's glaciers for decades, and satellite observations have played an important role in documenting their condition.

One of the earliest detailed surveys appeared in a 1982 study that used early Landsat satellite data, aerial photography, and topographic maps to examine the island's ice cover. Researchers identified four ice caps, along with rocky cliffs extending above the ice and glaciers flowing outward from the ice caps. Altogether, they documented 29 glaciers across Vega Island.

One of these, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been monitored in detail since the Antarctic summer of 1998-1999. Measurements collected over that period show an overall reduction in the glacier's mass.

The changes are not limited to Devil's Bay Glacier. Satellite observations spanning recent decades reveal that other glaciers on Vega Island have also lost ice, exposing increasing amounts of the underlying bedrock.

Long before satellites began monitoring its ice, Vega Island played an unexpected role in one of Antarctica's dramatic early exploration stories.

The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 traveled to the region to investigate the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding areas. What began as a scientific mission turned into a desperate struggle for survival.

During the expedition, the explorers became separated into three groups, each forced to endure the Antarctic winter in a different location. Their situation became even more dangerous when pack ice destroyed their ship, leaving them stranded in one of the world's most unforgiving environments.

Despite the ordeal, Vega Island eventually became the setting for a moment of hope. In spring 1903, two of the separated groups reunited at a location later named Cape Well-met, near what now resembles the “forehead” of the island's giant skull.

Not long afterward, an Argentinean expedition arrived and rescued the survivors, bringing their extraordinary Antarctic ordeal to an end.

Today, Vega Island remains a place where dramatic natural formations, a remarkable history of exploration, and the effects of a changing climate come together. Its ghostly skull may be one of Antarctica's most unusual sights, but the gradual transformation of the ice that shapes it tells an even more important story.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

#793. Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

Kane and Bellingham made their views clear at the review

England players are understood to have aired strong views about their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in a team meeting.

As BBC Sport reported in September, the Football Association (FA) process included canvassing the opinions of the squad - and it has emerged that took place at a 'full and frank' meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break.

BBC Sport has been told the squad feel that now they have been able to have their say, they can move on from their heartbreak in Atlanta on 15 July.

And this was demonstrated in the last international break when England, after a narrow defeat by Spain in the first game, went on to win the next three matches impressively.

Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.

Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.

As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.

Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.

Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.

Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.

It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.

There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.

That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.

There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.

All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.

As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.

Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.

Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.

If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.

Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.

"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.

"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."

We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

#792. Hota Kotb Details Co-Parenting Change With Ex Joel Schiffman

Hota Kotb gave an update on her co-parenting  dynamic with ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman, sharing it's now "more important than ever" to have daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, spend time with him.

Hoda Kotb is glad her ex Joel Schiffman will be there for their daughters today—and everyday.

The Today show alum to came a revelation about her co-parenting dynamic with the businessman—who she split from in 2022 following eight years of dating—after the two recently reunited to watch their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, take part in their school's Halloween parade.

“Usually, my kids wave and try to hide," Kotb shared as she filled in for Sheinelle Jones on the Nov. 9 episode of Today With Jenna & Sheinelle, adding that time time, "They saw Joel at the fence and beelined. They were saying to their friends, ‘That’s my dad,’ because they don't see him as much.”

“Whatever makes you different is hard, if your dad’s not there,” she continued. "I think there are a lot of kids who can relate. People will probably say, ‘Do you have a dad? Where is your dad?’ People ask them that."

For the 62-year-old, that exchange became a "very meaningful" moment in her motherhood journey as she realized the value in encouraging him to come more.

"As the girls are getting older, having their dad there is much more important than ever," Kotb explained. "When I was watching them say that, I thought, 'Oh my gosh, come all the time, be here as often as you can, because it matters.'"

All in all, Kotb said she and Schiffman—who dressed up in matching deviled eggs costumes to go trick-or-treating with their kids later that night—had a "lovely" time on Halloween.

"It was beautiful," she added. "He was on cloud nine. We all hung out. We barbecued."

But while Kotb and Schiffman, 68, work together on co-parenting, she believes their chapter as a couple has ended.

"Joel is one of the best people I know, and he really is a great human being," the Emmy winner raved on a 2024 episode of The Jamie Kern Lima Show. "And I feel like I'm a pretty great human being, but sometimes two great human beings together isn't quite enough to make it work."

Besides, Kotb recently struck up a connection with a man she met on a flight, who her former co-host Jenna Bush Hager jokingly called a "cute boy."

"Here's what I think of my future relationship life," Kotb shared after Bush Hager asked for updates on the Nov. 9 broadcast. "As I am going through life, there is going to be a person who shares more than just the things that matter to me when I was younger. I want someone with a deep spiritual connection, a deep emotional connection."

Though Kotb has admittedly been "scared" to date, she understands that she has to "take risks" in order to find love again.

"I‘m just keeping it as a thing," she added, "but truly, if I were to swallow a truth pill right now...I believe that the love part of my life is a piece that’s coming."

Blue Origin's big rocket is getting a little bigger.

Jeff Bezos' company announced today (Nov. 5) that it has developed a third stage for its New Glenn rocket, which it says will make the powerful launcher more capable and flexible.

The stage, called the GS3, "enhances New Glenn's capabilities," Blue Origin said in a blog post today. "The third stage enables direct deployment of satellite constellations to GEO [geostationary orbit] and supports heavy-lift science and exploration missions to the moon and deep space."

New Glenn is a two-stage vehicle at the moment. Its reusable first stage is powered by seven of Blue Origin's BE-4 engines, and its second stage features two of the company's BE-3Us. The rocket stands 322 feet (98 meters) tall and can haul 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) to geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) and 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit (LEO).

These are the specs for the standard, or "7x2," version of New Glenn. Last year, Blue Origin announced that it's developing a super-heavy variant known as the 9x4, because it will feature nine first-stage BE-4s and four upper-stage BE-3Us. The 9x4 will be nearly 400 feet (122 m) tall, and it will be able to loft 15.4 tons (14 metric tons) to GTO and 77 tons (70 metric tons) to LEO, according to Blue Origin.

New Glenn has flown three times to date, each time in the 7x2 configuration. The rocket debuted in January 2025, then launched again in November 2025 and again on April 19 of this year.

Things didn't go according to plan on that latest mission. The rocket deployed AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 communications satellite into the wrong orbit, and the spacecraft ended up being lost.

Another setback came just a month later: On May 28, New Glenn exploded on the pad during a routine engine test at Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Blue Origin has been working ever since to rebuild the pad and get New Glenn ready for its fourth flight, which is expected to occur late this year.

We now know that Blue Origin has also been working on the GS3 while those repairs were underway. The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. (The other is SpaceX's Starship.)

Blue Moon landing missions won't need to launch on GS3-equipped New Glenn rockets, according to Blue Origin. But the third stage "can support sustained operations around the moon," the company wrote in today's blog post. "By delivering significant payload mass directly to trans-lunar injection (TLI), GS3 enables faster transit times while preserving propellant for on-orbit operations."

And there's already demand for such services: Blue Origin also announced today that a government customer (which it did not name) has booked a GS3 mission to cislunar (Earth-moon) space, with launch targeted for 2028.

And the company dropped yet more news today — that it's working on a new first-stage engine, called Northstar.

Like Blue Origin's other booster engine, the BE-4, Northstar burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant, a combination known as methalox. But the new engine is more powerful and less complex.

"Compared to the BE-4 engine, Northstar reduces mass by 30% and parts count by 50%, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force," Blue Origin said in a second blog post today. "Manufacturing advancements have also significantly shortened production timelines, enabling assembly in less than a day."

Northstar went from program approval to development testing in just 11 months, according to the company. But today's update did not say when the new engine will fly for the first time.

#790. A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials

Scientists at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory have discovered that applying a small amount of pressure can dramatically alter the magnetic properties of a promising new class of materials called altermagnets. Using neutron experiments, the researchers uncovered how a simple mechanical squeeze can change the way these materials behave, offering a potential new approach to controlling magnetism.

The results, reported in two consecutive studies published in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, show that mechanical strain can influence both magnetic structures and the movement of electrons. This ability could provide a straightforward way to control materials being investigated for advanced electronic technologies.

Why Altermagnets Matter for Future Electronics

One particularly promising application involves spintronics, short for spin electronics. Unlike conventional electronics, which processes and stores information using the electrical charge of electrons, spintronics also takes advantage of a property known as electron spin.

If scientists can identify and develop suitable materials, including altermagnets, this approach could lead to major advances in technologies ranging from wireless communication to quantum computing.

"By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies," said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

A Simple Squeeze Reveals Surprising Magnetic Changes

To investigate how pressure affects these materials, the ORNL team placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between a pair of titanium plates and gently compressed them.

Using neutron diffraction at ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source, the scientists examined what happened to the magnetic structures inside the crystals. They found that the applied pressure changed the relative populations of magnetic domains, which are regions within a material that have particular magnetic arrangements. The strain also altered an electrical phenomenon called the anomalous Hall effect, providing evidence that the mechanical squeeze influenced the materials' electrical behavior.

"What's exciting is that one creative experimental idea -- a small mechanical squeeze between two plates -- can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism," said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author on both linked publications.

The findings highlight how a relatively simple experiment can uncover new ways to manipulate magnetic materials, potentially helping researchers develop the building blocks for future spintronic devices.

ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source is a DOE Office of Science user facility.

#789. Man Utd expected to sack head coach Carrick

Michael Carrick signed a two-year deal with Manchester United last summer

Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick.

The club opted to stick with Carrick after the side's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October, with the intention of reassessing the situation during this month's international break.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the board remain committed to that process, and that no final decision on Carrick's future has been made.

However, there is a growing expectation that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family for Carrick to be sacked.

The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

BBC Sport reported in October that the club had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick.

Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford.

Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August.

However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.

Man Utd score twice in stoppage-time to share points in eight-goal thriller

The Villa draw was Carrick's third match in charge since the club opted to give the 45-year-old more time at Old Trafford.

Results during that time - a win, a draw and a defeat - were mixed, and displayed the best and worst of Carrick's reign with United shipping goals but displaying good character to come back from two goals down on three occasions.

United's board toyed with sacking Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth, but decided the Englishman - and his players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around.

It was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.

Unfortunately for Carrick, it makes for poor reading.

With one victory in 10 Premier League matches, United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986/87 season.

They sit 18th in the table, one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace.

Only the Eagles and Ipswich have conceded more than the 19 goals United have shipped in the Premier League this season.

It is hard to believe given the club's current predicament just how quickly Carrick's tenure has soured.

Four 'huge mistakes' that show Man Utd's defensive problems

Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser.

The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.

After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton.

Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.

Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.

The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.

By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.

After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.

He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.

With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.
